Two Sum.mistake: Building the whole hash map in a first pass, then scanning again for target - x without comparing indices.
Two Sum.why: Two clean passes feel easier to reason about than mutating the map while you scan it, so the split looks like good hygiene.
Two Sum.consequence: An element pairs with itself: nums = [5, 2, 4], target = 10 finds the complement of 5 in the map — 5 at its own position — and returns [0, 0], which uses one element twice.
Two Sum.instead: Because the map should only ever contain indices you are allowed to pair with, do one pass and look up target - x before inserting x. The map then holds only earlier indices, and self-pairing becomes structurally impossible.

Two Sum.mistake: Sorting the array first and running two pointers, then returning the pointer positions.
Two Sum.why: Sorted-array-plus-two-pointers is the reflex for every pair-sum question, and it does find the right pair of values.
Two Sum.consequence: Sorting destroys the original indices: nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 sorts to [2, 3, 4], the pointers stop at positions 0 and 2, but the required answer is the original indices [1, 2].
Two Sum.instead: The problem asks for indices, not values, so any approach that reorders the array must carry the original positions along (sort pairs of value and index) — or skip sorting entirely and use the one-pass hash map.

Two Sum.mistake: Fixing the self-pair bug with a value check: skip the match whenever the complement equals the current number.
Two Sum.why: The broken case involved a number pairing with itself, so rejecting equal values looks like the surgical fix.
Two Sum.consequence: nums = [3, 3], target = 6 has a valid answer using two different indices that hold equal values, and the value guard rejects it, so the function returns nothing.
Two Sum.instead: Identity here means index, not value — two distinct positions may hold the same number. Compare indices, or structure the loop (lookup before insert) so a same-index collision cannot occur in the first place.

Two Sum.mistake: Coding the nested-loop brute force and stopping once the sample tests pass.
Two Sum.why: It is correct, it takes two minutes to write, and the interviewer has not objected yet, so it feels safe to move on.
Two Sum.consequence: At scale it dies: nums = list(range(100000)) with target = 199997 forces roughly 5 * 10^9 comparisons in the O(n^2) scan and times out on any judge.
Two Sum.instead: Interviewers expect the brute force named, not submitted. Say it in one sentence, then state the trade you are making — a hash map spends O(n) extra space to cut lookup of the complement to O(1), giving O(n) total — and code that.

3 Sum.mistake: Skipping duplicate values only at the outer anchor index, not at the two inner pointers after recording a hit.
3 Sum.why: Duplicate triplets seem to come from repeating the anchor element, so deduplicating the anchor feels like the whole job.
3 Sum.consequence: nums = [-2, 0, 0, 2, 2]: after finding [-2, 0, 2], the left and right pointers land on the second 0 and second 2 and emit [-2, 0, 2] again — the output contains the same triplet twice.
3 Sum.instead: Every position that can repeat a value needs its own skip. After recording a triplet, advance left past all equal neighbors (while nums[left] == nums[left + 1]) and do the same on the right before continuing.

3 Sum.mistake: Deduplicating the anchor by looking ahead — skip index i when nums[i] equals nums[i + 1].
3 Sum.why: Looking ahead and looking back both appear to remove repeated anchors, so the direction of the comparison feels arbitrary.
3 Sum.consequence: nums = [-1, -1, 0, 1, 2]: the look-ahead skip discards the first -1 before it can pair with the second, so the valid triplet [-1, -1, 2] is never found.
3 Sum.instead: The first occurrence must be the one that runs, because only it can still see every later element, including its own duplicates. Skip i only when i > 0 and nums[i] equals nums[i - 1] — compare backward, not forward.

3 Sum.mistake: Running the O(n^3) triple loop and throwing triplets into a set to deduplicate.
3 Sum.why: A set feels like a shortcut around the fiddly pointer-skipping logic, and it does produce correct output on small cases.
3 Sum.consequence: With the classic constraint n = 3000, the triple loop performs about 2.7 * 10^10 iterations and times out; hashing a sorted copy of every candidate triplet adds even more cost on top.
3 Sum.instead: Sorting is what makes deduplication cheap: after an O(n log n) sort, duplicates sit adjacent, so skipping them is a single comparison, and the same sortedness enables the O(n^2) two-pointer scan. One preprocessing step buys both properties.

3 Sum.mistake: Breaking out of the two-pointer scan as soon as one triplet is found for the current anchor.
3 Sum.why: Two Sum trains the habit that one answer per search is enough, and the pattern carries over without being re-examined.
3 Sum.consequence: nums = [-4, 0, 1, 3, 4] (sorted): anchor -4 needs pairs summing to 4, and both (0, 4) and (1, 3) qualify — breaking after the first emits [-4, 0, 4] but silently drops [-4, 1, 3].
3 Sum.instead: A fixed anchor can complete several distinct triplets, so after each hit move both pointers inward (past duplicates) and keep scanning until they cross. The loop ends when the pointers meet, not when the first answer appears.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.mistake: Initializing the best answer to 0, or resetting the running sum to 0 as the floor.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.why: An empty subarray summing to 0 feels like a harmless safe default, and it works on every test containing a positive number.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.consequence: An all-negative array breaks it: nums = [-3, -1, -2] must return -1, the largest single element, but the 0-floored version returns 0 — the sum of a subarray that does not exist.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.instead: The subarray must be non-empty, so seed both best and current with nums[0] and start the loop at index 1. The extension rule is current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]): restart at the element itself, never at zero.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.mistake: Resetting the running sum whenever the current element is negative.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.why: Negative numbers look like pure damage, so cutting the subarray the moment one appears feels like the obvious defensive move.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.consequence: nums = [4, -1, 5]: resetting at -1 splits the array into pieces worth 4 and 5, returning 5, while the true answer is 8 from carrying [4, -1, 5] whole.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.instead: A negative element is worth carrying when the sum before it is positive enough to absorb it. The correct trigger is the running sum itself going negative — a negative prefix drags down every extension — not the sign of one element.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.mistake: Assuming Kadane transfers unchanged to the maximum product subarray variant.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.why: The two problems share the same shape — scan once, keep a running best ending here — so the substitution feels mechanical.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.consequence: nums = [-2, 3, -4]: a single running maximum ends at 3, but the true maximum product is 24 from the whole array, because two negatives multiply into a positive.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.instead: Name the invariant Kadane depends on: under addition, a discarded prefix can never help later. Multiplication breaks that — a terrible product can flip into the best one — so the product variant must track the minimum and maximum ending at each index.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.mistake: Memorizing the two-line loop without being able to argue why discarding a negative prefix is safe.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.why: The code is famous, short, and passes every test, so a proof feels like decoration rather than substance.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.consequence: On nums = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4], the interviewer asks why resetting before the 4 cannot lose a better answer — and with no invariant to point to, the follow-up stalls even though the code was right.
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.instead: State the invariant out loud: current is the best sum of any subarray ending at index i. A prefix whose sum is negative lowers every subarray it starts, so dropping it can never hurt — one sentence, and the follow-up is handled.

Sort Colors.mistake: Advancing the mid pointer after swapping with the high pointer.
Sort Colors.why: The low-side swap does advance mid, and making the two branches symmetric feels tidy and consistent.
Sort Colors.consequence: nums = [1, 2, 0]: mid meets the 2, swaps with high to get [1, 0, 2], and if mid advances, the 0 that arrived at index 1 is never examined — the array ends as [1, 0, 2].
Sort Colors.instead: The element swapped in from the high side is a stranger you have not classified yet, so mid must stay put and look at it. After a low-side swap the incoming element was already scanned, which is exactly why advancing is safe there.

Sort Colors.mistake: Writing the loop condition as mid < high instead of mid <= high.
Sort Colors.why: Most two-pointer loops stop when the pointers meet, so the strict inequality is muscle memory.
Sort Colors.consequence: nums = [2, 0, 1]: after the first swap the state is [1, 0, 2] with mid = 1 and high = 1, the strict loop exits, and the unclassified 0 at index 1 leaves the array as [1, 0, 2].
Sort Colors.instead: The cell at high has not been examined until mid passes it — the invariant covers [0, low) as zeros, [low, mid) as ones, and (high, end] as twos, leaving [mid, high] unknown. Run while mid <= high so the unknown region empties completely.

Sort Colors.mistake: Reaching for the built-in sort, or counting the three values in one pass and rewriting in a second.
Sort Colors.why: Both are correct, quick to write, and hard to get wrong under pressure, so they feel like the pragmatic choice.
Sort Colors.consequence: Nothing fails functionally on nums = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0], but the stated constraint — one pass, constant extra space, no library sort — is the actual question being asked (the Dutch national flag partition), and both answers sidestep it.
Sort Colors.instead: Offer counting as the warm-up in one sentence, then present the three-pointer partition and say its invariant aloud. The interviewer is grading whether you can maintain a multi-region invariant, not whether you can call sort().

Next Permutation.mistake: After finding the pivot (the first index from the right where the value increases), swapping it with the largest element to its right.
Next Permutation.why: The goal is to make the number bigger, and grabbing the biggest available digit sounds like the way to do that.
Next Permutation.consequence: nums = [1, 3, 2]: the pivot is 1, and swapping with the largest suffix element 3 gives [3, 1, 2] — but the next permutation is [2, 1, 3], the smallest arrangement greater than [1, 3, 2].
Next Permutation.instead: Next means the minimal possible increase, so swap the pivot with the smallest element to its right that is still greater than it — the rightmost such element, since the suffix is descending — and then make the suffix as small as possible.

Next Permutation.mistake: Swapping the pivot correctly but forgetting to reverse the suffix afterward.
Next Permutation.why: The swap is the step that makes the number bigger, so it feels like the finish line; the reversal reads like optional cleanup.
Next Permutation.consequence: nums = [1, 5, 4, 3, 2]: swapping pivot 1 with 2 gives [2, 5, 4, 3, 1] and stops there, but the correct answer is [2, 1, 3, 4, 5] — without the reversal you return a much larger permutation than the next one.
Next Permutation.instead: After the swap, the suffix is still in descending order, which is the largest arrangement of those digits. Reversing it makes it ascending — the smallest — which is what makes the overall result the immediate next permutation rather than a distant one.

Next Permutation.mistake: Not handling the fully descending array, where no pivot exists.
Next Permutation.why: Every walked-through example has a pivot, so the scan running off the left end never comes up until it crashes.
Next Permutation.consequence: nums = [3, 2, 1] has no next permutation; the spec says wrap around to the sorted order [1, 2, 3], but code that assumes a pivot indexes position -1 or returns the array unchanged.
Next Permutation.instead: Treat the failed scan as a signal, not an error: when the whole array is non-increasing, reverse it entirely and return. This is the wrap-around case, and interviewers check it deliberately.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.mistake: Counting upward from every element with set lookups, without first checking that the element starts a sequence.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.why: The hash set makes each membership test O(1), so the whole thing feels like it must already be linear.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.consequence: nums = list(range(100000)): every element launches a walk to the end of the run, so the walks cost 100000 + 99999 + ... — an O(n^2) blowup on exactly the input the problem advertises, and it times out.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.instead: Only start walking from sequence starts — elements x where x - 1 is not in the set. Every run is then traversed once from its left end, each element is touched a bounded number of times, and the O(n) claim becomes true.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.mistake: Sorting and counting streaks, but resetting the streak when two equal neighbors appear.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.why: The counting loop compares adjacent elements, and a duplicate is neither one bigger nor part of an increase, so the reset branch swallows it.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.consequence: nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]: the second 2 resets the counter, so the reported answer is 2 while the real consecutive run 1, 2, 3 has length 3.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.instead: Duplicates should be invisible: skip equal neighbors and reset only when the gap exceeds 1 — or deduplicate through a set before sorting. Also say aloud that sorting makes this O(n log n), since the follow-up will ask for O(n).

Longest Consecutive Sequence.mistake: Reading consecutive as adjacent-in-the-array and finding the longest increasing-by-one subarray.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.why: The word consecutive strongly suggests positions, and most array questions do care about contiguity, so the misreading feels natural.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.consequence: nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]: no two adjacent cells differ by one, so the subarray reading returns 1, while the intended answer is 4 for the scattered values 1, 2, 3, 4.
Longest Consecutive Sequence.instead: Consecutive here describes values, and array order is irrelevant — which is why a set is the right container. Restate the problem to the interviewer in your own words before coding; this one is worded to invite the wrong reading.

Set Matrix Zeroes.mistake: Zeroing out rows and columns immediately, during the same scan that discovers the zeros.
Set Matrix Zeroes.why: Discover-and-act in one pass feels efficient, and on many inputs the corruption happens to stay invisible.
Set Matrix Zeroes.consequence: matrix = [[0, 1], [1, 1]]: zeroing row 0 and column 0 on discovery writes a new 0 at position (0, 1), the scan then treats it as original and zeroes column 1, and the whole matrix becomes 0 instead of [[0, 0], [0, 1]].
Set Matrix Zeroes.instead: The zeros you write must never be confused with the zeros you found, so separate the phases: first record which rows and columns are condemned, then apply the zeroing in a second pass.

Set Matrix Zeroes.mistake: Using the first row and column as marker space for O(1) memory, but letting matrix[0][0] serve as the flag for both of them.
Set Matrix Zeroes.why: The two flag roles collide in a single cell, and on most inputs the collision never gets exercised, so the bug hides through testing.
Set Matrix Zeroes.consequence: matrix = [[1, 2], [0, 4]]: the zero at (1, 0) marks column 0 by setting matrix[0][0] = 0; the apply phase reads matrix[0][0] == 0 as row 0 was condemned too, and the output becomes [[0, 0], [0, 0]] instead of [[0, 2], [0, 0]].
Set Matrix Zeroes.instead: Give one of the two roles its own boolean stored outside the matrix, mark everything else in the first row and column, and apply to the interior first, the first row and column last — order of application is exactly what the interviewer probes.

Set Matrix Zeroes.mistake: Answering with the O(m + n) row-set and column-set version and treating the problem as finished.
Set Matrix Zeroes.why: It is clean, correct, and quick to write, and it passes every functional test, so it reads as the complete solution.
Set Matrix Zeroes.consequence: Nothing breaks functionally, but on the stated follow-up — constant extra space for a matrix near 200 x 200 with m + n auxiliary flags disallowed — the answer is exactly what the problem told you not to settle for, e.g. constraints like m, n <= 200 with O(1) space required.
Set Matrix Zeroes.instead: Present the set version as the baseline in one sentence, then walk to the refinement: the first row and column can store the flags in place. The migration from O(m + n) to O(1) is the whole interview here.

Rotate Matrix.mistake: Transposing by looping over every (i, j) pair instead of only the upper triangle.
Rotate Matrix.why: Transpose means swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i], and looping over everything looks like the direct translation of that sentence.
Rotate Matrix.consequence: matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]: the pair (0, 1) is swapped when the loop visits (0, 1) and swapped back when it visits (1, 0), so the transpose is a no-op and the final answer is only a row reversal — not a rotation.
Rotate Matrix.instead: Each pair must be exchanged exactly once, so restrict the inner loop to j > i. Off-diagonal cells then get one swap each and the diagonal is left alone.

Rotate Matrix.mistake: Reversing each column after the transpose instead of each row.
Rotate Matrix.why: After transposing, some reversal finishes the rotation, and rows versus columns is a 50/50 guess that both look plausible on paper.
Rotate Matrix.consequence: matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]: transpose gives [[1, 3], [2, 4]]; reversing columns produces [[2, 4], [1, 3]], which is the counterclockwise rotation — the clockwise answer is [[3, 1], [4, 2]] from reversing rows.
Rotate Matrix.instead: Fix the orientation with a two-second test before coding: in a clockwise rotation the top-left corner (0, 0) must land at the top-right (0, n-1). Run the 2x2 by hand; clockwise is transpose then reverse each row.

Rotate Matrix.mistake: Writing the four-way cyclic swap with hand-derived layer indices from memory.
Rotate Matrix.why: The ring-by-ring swap feels like the real in-place solution, and deriving indices live seems like a chance to look thorough.
Rotate Matrix.consequence: One off-by-one in the layer bounds on matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] — such as letting the inner loop include the layer's last cell — rotates a corner twice and silently corrupts the matrix, and debugging four coupled indices live burns the remaining time.
Rotate Matrix.instead: Transpose plus reverse-rows is equally in-place and O(1) extra, and each half can be verified independently on a 2x2. Under interview pressure, prefer the decomposition whose steps you can check in isolation.

Majority Element (> n/2 times).mistake: Running Boyer-Moore voting and returning the surviving candidate without a verification pass.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).why: On the classic version the majority element is guaranteed to exist, so the candidate is always right and the verify pass looks like dead code.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).consequence: nums = [1, 2, 3] has no majority: the vote still ends with some candidate (here 3), which appears once — far short of more than n/2 = 1.5 — and returning it is wrong the moment the guarantee is dropped.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).instead: State the contract precisely: the voting pass proves only that no element other than the candidate can be the majority. When existence is not promised, a second O(n) counting pass confirms count > n/2 before you return.

Majority Element (> n/2 times).mistake: Keeping the old candidate when the counter reaches zero instead of adopting the current element.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).why: The candidate has survived this far, so holding onto it while the count goes negative feels like loyalty to the front-runner.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).consequence: nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2]: the count for candidate 1 reaches zero after four elements; without replacement the final answer stays 1, while the true majority is 2.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).instead: A zero counter means the prefix so far has fully canceled out — pairs of different values eliminated each other — so the slate is clean. Adopt the current element as the new candidate; the majority element survives every such cancellation.

Majority Element (> n/2 times).mistake: Counting occurrences in a hash map and returning the max, without acknowledging the space constraint.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).why: It is the first correct idea that comes to mind, and for most jobs it would be the right engineering call.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).consequence: Nothing is wrong functionally, but with n = 10^7 elements the map can grow to millions of entries while the follow-up demands O(1) space — and the interviewer chose this problem specifically for that follow-up.
Majority Element (> n/2 times).instead: Offer the map as the baseline, then explain the voting insight: removing a pair of two different values never changes which element holds the majority, so a single counter and candidate suffice. Naming that invariant is the answer.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.mistake: Comparing only adjacent intervals in the given order, without sorting first.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.why: The examples in the prompt often arrive nearly sorted, so a single adjacent-pair pass appears to work on everything you test.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.consequence: intervals = [[1, 4], [5, 6], [0, 10]]: the adjacent check merges [5, 6] into [0, 10] but never revisits [1, 4], leaving [[1, 4], [0, 10]] where the correct output is [[0, 10]] alone.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.instead: Sorting by start is what makes one pass sufficient: after the sort, every interval that can merge with the current group is contiguous with it, so a single sweep with a growing current interval is provably complete.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.mistake: Using a strict comparison for overlap, so intervals that touch at an endpoint stay separate.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.why: Overlap intuitively means sharing interior points, and [1, 4] next to [4, 5] feels like touching rather than overlapping.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.consequence: intervals = [[1, 4], [4, 5]]: with current.start < last.end the two are left apart, producing [[1, 4], [4, 5]] where the expected answer is [[1, 5]] — touching intervals merge in the standard version.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.instead: This is a specification question, not a coding one: ask whether closed intervals sharing an endpoint should merge, state that the standard convention uses <=, and encode the agreed rule deliberately.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.mistake: On a merge, assigning the new end from the current interval instead of taking the max.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.why: The list is sorted by start, so the later interval feels like it must also reach further right.
Merge Overlapping Intervals.consequence: intervals = [[1, 10], [2, 3]]: blind assignment shrinks the merged end from 10 to 3, and the output [[1, 3]] silently loses the coverage from 4 to 10 — the correct answer is [[1, 10]].
Merge Overlapping Intervals.instead: Sorting by start says nothing about ends: an interval can be entirely contained in the previous one. Always extend with max(last.end, current.end), and test with a contained interval to prove it to yourself.

Find Duplicate Number.mistake: Sorting the array or inserting everything into a set to find the repeat.
Find Duplicate Number.why: Both are the natural first instincts for duplicate detection, and both produce the right number on any test input.
Find Duplicate Number.consequence: nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2] with the stated constraints — the array is read-only and extra space must be O(1) — rules both out: sorting mutates the input, and a set costs O(n) space, so the answer fails the actual problem even though the output is right.
Find Duplicate Number.instead: Read the constraints as the puzzle: values in 1..n mean nums[i] can be treated as a pointer to index nums[i], turning the array into a linked structure where the duplicate value is a cycle entrance — which Floyd's two-pointer cycle finding locates in O(1) space.

Find Duplicate Number.mistake: Starting both of Floyd's pointers at the same place and testing slow == fast before either has moved.
Find Duplicate Number.why: The linked-list version of the loop transfers by copy-paste, and the pointers being equal at the start looks harmless.
Find Duplicate Number.consequence: nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]: with slow = fast = 0 and a while (slow != fast) loop, the condition is false immediately, the loop body never runs, and phase two returns a value from an unmoved state — the wrong answer.
Find Duplicate Number.instead: Advance before comparing: use a do-while shape, or start slow = nums[0] and fast = nums[nums[0]] so the first comparison happens after real movement. Then the meeting point is meaningful and phase two (reset one pointer to the start, step both singly) finds the entrance.

Find Duplicate Number.mistake: Binary searching on the value range with the counting comparison pointed the wrong way.
Find Duplicate Number.why: Count how many elements are at most mid is easy to compute, but which half the duplicate lives in is easy to invert in your head.
Find Duplicate Number.consequence: nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2] with mid = 2: three elements are <= 2, which exceeds mid, proving the duplicate lies in 1..2 — the flipped comparison walks to 3..4 instead and returns a value that appears once.
Find Duplicate Number.instead: Anchor the code to the pigeonhole invariant: n + 1 numbers occupy n value-slots, so whichever half is overcrowded contains the duplicate — count(x <= mid) > mid means go low. Write the invariant as a comment first, then the comparison cannot flip.

Buy and Sell Stock.mistake: Finding the global minimum and global maximum of the prices and returning their difference.
Buy and Sell Stock.why: Buy at the all-time low, sell at the all-time high sounds exactly like what maximizing profit means.
Buy and Sell Stock.consequence: prices = [7, 6, 4, 3, 1]: the maximum 7 is on day 0 and the minimum 1 is on day 4, so the sell would happen before the buy; the min-max difference is meaningless and the correct answer is 0.
Buy and Sell Stock.instead: Time only flows forward, so the constraint is order: while scanning, keep the minimum price seen so far and measure today's price against it. The best profit is the best such difference, floored at 0.

Buy and Sell Stock.mistake: Summing every upward price move, which solves the unlimited-transactions variant instead.
Buy and Sell Stock.why: The stock problems blur together after enough practice, and collecting every rise genuinely is optimal when you may trade repeatedly.
Buy and Sell Stock.consequence: prices = [1, 3, 2, 4]: summing upticks gives (3 - 1) + (4 - 2) = 4, but this problem allows one transaction, so the correct answer is 3 — buy at 1, sell at 4.
Buy and Sell Stock.instead: Confirm which member of the family you are solving before coding: one transaction, unlimited, at most k, or with cooldown all have different recurrences. Saying the family out loud is itself a signal interviewers look for.

Buy and Sell Stock.mistake: Returning the best difference even when every possible trade loses money.
Buy and Sell Stock.why: Initializing the answer with the first computed difference, or with negative infinity, is standard practice in max-tracking loops.
Buy and Sell Stock.consequence: prices = [5, 3, 1]: every buy-sell pair is a loss, the best difference is -2, and the code returns -2 where the problem specifies 0 — decline to trade rather than trade at a loss.
Buy and Sell Stock.instead: Initialize best profit to 0 so not trading is always on the table, and confirm with the interviewer that a forced transaction is not intended. Degenerate inputs like strictly falling prices are exactly what they will test.

Trapping Rain Water.mistake: Computing the water above each bar against the single global maximum height.
Trapping Rain Water.why: Water fills up to the tallest wall is the mental picture, and one global ceiling feels like a clean formalization of it.
Trapping Rain Water.consequence: height = [3, 0, 2]: the global max is 3, so index 1 is credited 3 - 0 = 3 units of water, but the right wall is only 2 high, so 1 unit spills over the right — the true answer is 2.
Trapping Rain Water.instead: Each column holds water up to the shorter of the tallest wall on its left and the tallest on its right: water[i] = min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) - height[i]. The bound is local to the column, not global.

Trapping Rain Water.mistake: Building the leftMax and rightMax arrays excluding the bar itself, then summing min minus height without a floor.
Trapping Rain Water.why: A wall to the left of me reads as strictly left, so excluding the current bar from its own maximum feels more precise, not less.
Trapping Rain Water.consequence: height = [1, 5, 1]: excluding self, the bar of height 5 sees walls of height 1 on both sides, contributing min(1, 1) - 5 = -4, and the total goes negative instead of 0.
Trapping Rain Water.instead: Define leftMax[i] as the maximum over height[0..i] inclusive; then min(leftMax, rightMax) - height[i] is non-negative by construction and no clamping is needed. Choosing definitions that make bad states unrepresentable beats patching with max(0, ...).

Trapping Rain Water.mistake: In the two-pointer version, processing whichever side is taller and crediting water from that side's running max.
Trapping Rain Water.why: The two branches look symmetric, and processing the impressive tall side feels like it should be at least as safe.
Trapping Rain Water.consequence: height = [2, 0, 3, 0, 1]: the true answer is 3, but crediting a column from the taller side's max uses a wall the scan has not yet confirmed on the other side, overfilling the pit at index 3 and returning 4.
Trapping Rain Water.instead: Always process the shorter side, because its running max is a proven bound: the other side is already known to be at least as tall, so min of the two walls is settled. That one sentence is the correctness argument interviewers want to hear.

Trapping Rain Water.mistake: In the monotonic-stack version, computing the trapped width without subtracting one for the walls.
Trapping Rain Water.why: Distance between two indices is right minus left everywhere else, so the extra minus one reads like a typo rather than a necessity.
Trapping Rain Water.consequence: height = [2, 0, 2]: popping the 0 with left wall at index 0 and right wall at index 2, the water spans width 2 - 0 - 1 = 1 for an answer of 2; dropping the minus one doubles it to 4.
Trapping Rain Water.instead: The water sits strictly between the two walls, so the width is right - left - 1. Verify the formula once on the three-bar case [2, 0, 2], where the answer must be 2, before trusting the stack version.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.mistake: Testing which half is sorted with a strict comparison, nums[lo] < nums[mid].
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.why: Strict and non-strict feel interchangeable when you picture a long sorted run, because ties seem like a non-event.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.consequence: nums = [3, 1], target = 1: lo and mid are both index 0, the strict test fails, the code declares the right half sorted, concludes 1 is not in it, and searches left — returning -1 for a present element.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.instead: When lo equals mid, the left half is a single element and is sorted by definition, so the test must be nums[lo] <= nums[mid]. Hand-run both two-element rotations, [3, 1] and [1, 3], before trusting the loop.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.mistake: Running ordinary binary search, steering only by comparing the target to nums[mid].
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.why: The array is described as sorted, and one rotation feels like a detail the comparisons will absorb.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.consequence: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0: plain binary search sees 0 < 7 at the midpoint and goes left, but 0 lives in the right half — the search returns -1.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.instead: Rotation means one half is always sorted and the other contains the seam. First identify the sorted half (nums[lo] <= nums[mid] means it is the left), then ask whether the target lies within that half's value range; go there if yes, to the other half if no.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.mistake: Testing membership in the sorted half with strict inequalities on both ends.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.why: The midpoint is checked separately for equality, so excluding both boundaries from the range test feels consistent.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.consequence: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 4: the left half is sorted and 4 sits exactly at nums[lo], but the strict test 4 < target rejects it, the search bounces right, and the function returns -1 for the element at index 0.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.instead: The boundaries belong to the sorted half, so the range test is nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid] (with the mid equality handled first). Targets equal to an endpoint are the classic off-by-one here — test them deliberately.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.mistake: Merging the two arrays completely and indexing into the middle.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.why: It is correct, you already know how to merge sorted arrays, and the median definition points straight at the middle element.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.consequence: With two arrays of 10^6 elements each, the merge costs O(m + n) time and space while the problem explicitly demands O(log(min(m, n))) — the interviewer treats the merge as the baseline, not the answer, and the clock is gone.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.instead: Name the merge in one sentence as the baseline, then reframe: the median is a partition of the combined data into equal halves where every left element is <= every right element, and that partition point can be binary searched.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.mistake: Binary searching the partition over the larger array instead of the smaller one.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.why: The arrays feel interchangeable — both are sorted inputs to a symmetric formula — so which one hosts the search reads as a coin flip.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.consequence: nums1 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], nums2 = [5]: half of the total is 5, and searching i over 0..8 in nums1 makes the complementary cut j = 5 - i go negative (i = 8 gives j = -3), indexing out of bounds.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.instead: The complementary cut j = half - i stays within 0..len(nums2) only when the search space i is the smaller array — that is the reason the algorithm runs on min(m, n), not a micro-optimization. Say the reason, then code it.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.mistake: Reading partition neighbors at the array edges without infinity sentinels.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.why: The formula reads nums1[i - 1] and nums1[i] so uniformly that the edge cuts i = 0 and i = m look like they will take care of themselves.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.consequence: nums1 = [5], nums2 = [1, 2, 3]: at the cut i = 0, Python evaluates nums1[-1] as the last element 5 instead of negative infinity, silently steering the search the wrong way; at i = 1, reading nums1[1] raises IndexError.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.instead: Model the empty side of a cut explicitly: left neighbor is -infinity when i = 0, right neighbor is +infinity when i = m. In Python, negative indexing makes the missing-sentinel bug silent rather than crashing, which makes it worse.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.mistake: Mixing conventions between the left-half size and the odd-total return value.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.why: Both (m + n) // 2 and (m + n + 1) // 2 appear in references, and both max-of-left and min-of-right appear as the odd-case answer, so a mismatched pairing looks plausible.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.consequence: nums1 = [1, 3], nums2 = [2]: with the left half sized (m + n + 1) // 2 = 2, the odd-total median is max of the left halves, which is 2; pairing that sizing with a min-of-right return gives 3 instead.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.instead: Pick one convention and state it: the left half carries the extra element, so an odd total returns max(left1, left2). Verify the pairing on the three-element case [1, 3] and [2], where the median must be 2, before generalizing.

Pow(x, n).mistake: Handling a negative exponent by negating n and inverting at the end, with fixed-width integers.
Pow(x, n).why: pow(x, -n) equals 1 / pow(x, n), so negate-then-recurse feels like a complete treatment of the negative case.
Pow(x, n).consequence: x = 2, n = -2147483648: in a 32-bit int, negating -2^31 overflows because 2^31 is unrepresentable, giving an infinite loop or wrong sign in C++ or Java; the input is a standard test.
Pow(x, n).instead: Widen before negating (use a 64-bit copy of n), or fold the sign into the recurrence. Python cannot overflow here, but say the caveat aloud — the interviewer is checking whether you know where the trap lives, not whether your language dodges it.

Pow(x, n).mistake: Writing the recursion as pow(x, n / 2) * pow(x, n / 2), calling the half twice.
Pow(x, n).why: The identity x^n = x^(n/2) * x^(n/2) is exactly what the math says, and transcribing math directly into code feels safe.
Pow(x, n).consequence: Two recursive calls per level makes the call tree full: x = 2, n = 1024 triggers 2047 calls instead of 11, and at n near 10^9 the O(n) blowup times out — the divide-and-conquer gained nothing.
Pow(x, n).instead: The speedup comes from reuse, not from splitting: bind half = pow(x, n // 2) once, return half * half (times x when n is odd). One extra local variable is the entire difference between O(log n) and O(n).

Pow(x, n).mistake: In the iterative bit-by-bit version, squaring the base but mishandling the multiply on odd bits.
Pow(x, n).why: The loop is short and rhythmic — square, shift, repeat — and the conditional multiply feels like a detail the rhythm will carry.
Pow(x, n).consequence: x = 2, n = 3: with the odd-bit multiply dropped or misplaced, the result never absorbs the base and comes out as 1 or 4 instead of 8 — wrong on the smallest odd exponent.
Pow(x, n).instead: Carry the loop invariant explicitly: answer * base^n stays constant across every iteration. Check it by hand on n = 3 — if the invariant holds at each of the two steps, the conditional multiply is in the right place.

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.mistake: On seeing a repeated character, resetting the window to start at the current position.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.why: A repeat feels like a dead end, and starting fresh from where you stand seems like the clean recovery.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.consequence: s = 'dvdf': at the second d the window restarts at index 2, producing df of length 2, but the correct answer is 3 — the window vdf remains valid because the first d could have been dropped alone.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.instead: Only the prefix up to and including the previous occurrence of the repeated character is invalid; everything after it is still good. Shrink the left edge to one past that occurrence and keep the rest of the window.

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.mistake: Jumping the window start to last[c] + 1 without checking that the stored occurrence is inside the current window.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.why: The last-seen map gives an exact position, and moving the start there reads like the precise version of shrinking.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.consequence: s = 'abba': at the final a, last['a'] is 0, so start jumps backward from 2 to 1 and the window pretends bba has no repeat — reporting length 3 where the correct answer is 2.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.instead: The window's left edge must never move left, because positions behind it are already excluded. Guard the jump with start = max(start, last[c] + 1), and note that stale map entries are exactly what the max is defending against.

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.mistake: Updating the best length only inside the repeat-handling branch.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.why: Repeats are where the interesting events happen, so the bookkeeping gravitates there and the quiet path gets forgotten.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.consequence: s = 'abc': no repeat ever fires, the best-length update never runs, and the function returns 0 for a string whose answer is 3.
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.instead: The window is valid at the end of every iteration, so measure it every iteration: best = max(best, i - start + 1) on each step. Inputs with no repeats at all are the first edge case to test.

Longest Palindromic Substring.mistake: Expanding around single-character centers only, ignoring the gaps between characters.
Longest Palindromic Substring.why: A palindrome mirrors around its middle, and picturing a middle character is far more natural than picturing a middle gap.
Longest Palindromic Substring.consequence: s = 'cbbd': the answer bb has even length, so its center is the gap between the two b characters; odd-only expansion returns a single letter of length 1 instead of bb.
Longest Palindromic Substring.instead: Enumerate all 2n - 1 centers — every character and every gap between adjacent characters — expanding each. Even-length palindromes exist, and their centers are gaps; building that into the loop costs one extra call per index.

Longest Palindromic Substring.mistake: Reversing the string and taking the longest common substring with the original.
Longest Palindromic Substring.why: A palindrome reads the same both ways, so the longest stretch shared with the reversal feels like exactly the right object.
Longest Palindromic Substring.consequence: s = 'abacdfgdcaba': the reversal shares the 5-character block 'abacd', which is not a palindrome — the mirrored copy comes from the other end of the string, not the same position; the true answer is 'aba'.
Longest Palindromic Substring.instead: A shared block only certifies a palindrome when it maps back to the same indices, so the reduction needs an index check bolted on. Expand-around-center gives O(n^2) with no such trap and O(1) space — prefer the approach whose correctness needs no patch.

Longest Palindromic Substring.mistake: Filling the interval DP table in ascending row order, reading dp[i + 1][j - 1] before it exists.
Longest Palindromic Substring.why: Row-by-row is the default order for filling any 2D table, and the recurrence looks like every other DP transition.
Longest Palindromic Substring.consequence: s = 'babad': deciding dp[0][2] for 'bab' consults dp[1][1], which ascending row order has not computed yet, so 'bab' is missed and the reported answer collapses to a single character like 'b'.
Longest Palindromic Substring.instead: A palindrome's truth depends on a shorter substring inside it, so the table must be filled by increasing substring length (or with i descending). In interval DP, the iteration order is part of the correctness argument — state it before writing the loops.

Coin Change.mistake: Greedily taking the largest coin that still fits, repeatedly.
Coin Change.why: It is how humans make change, and it genuinely is optimal for canonical currency systems like 1, 5, 10, 25.
Coin Change.consequence: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 for three coins, while the optimum is 3 + 3 with two — greedy has no exchange argument for arbitrary denominations.
Coin Change.instead: Arbitrary coin systems need the DP over amounts: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over usable coins c. Mention that greedy works for canonical systems and name a counterexample set like [1, 3, 4] — that contrast is a favorite probe.

Coin Change.mistake: Marking unreachable amounts with 0 or -1 inside the dp array and letting them join the min.
Coin Change.why: 0 and -1 are the reflexive null values, and the initialization line gets written before the transition is thought through.
Coin Change.consequence: coins = [2], amount = 3: dp[1] is unreachable, but stored as 0 it offers dp[3] = dp[1] + 1 = 1 — claiming amount 3 is makeable with one coin when the correct answer is -1.
Coin Change.instead: Unreachable must mean infinitely expensive so the min ignores it: seed dp[0] = 0 and everything else with infinity (amount + 1 works as a practical infinity), then translate a still-infinite dp[amount] to -1 at the end.

Coin Change.mistake: Agonizing over whether the coin loop or the amount loop goes outside, without knowing when it matters.
Coin Change.why: The counting variant of this problem genuinely depends on loop order, and the two problems blur into each other after enough practice.
Coin Change.consequence: For min-coins both orders give the same answer, so nothing fails here — but in the counting variant, coins = [1, 2], amount = 3 yields 2 combinations with coins outside and 3 ordered sequences with amounts outside, and interviewers ask you to explain exactly this contrast.
Coin Change.instead: Know the reason, not the ritual: min() gives the same result no matter how many times a candidate is offered, so order is free here; counting sums contributions, where order changes what is counted. Being able to say that sentence is the point.

Coin Change.mistake: Writing top-down memoization on (index, amount) but moving to index - 1 after taking a coin.
Coin Change.why: The 0/1 knapsack template is burned in, and advancing the index after a take is its signature move.
Coin Change.consequence: coins = [2], amount = 4: advancing the index after taking the 2 allows each coin at most once, so the search never builds 2 + 2 and returns -1 where the correct answer is 2 coins.
Coin Change.instead: Unbounded supply is encoded by where the recursion goes after a take: stay at the same index (take again is allowed), and advance only on skip. One index expresses the entire difference between 0/1 and unbounded — point at it explicitly.

Edit Distance.mistake: Initializing the first row and first column of the DP table to zeros.
Edit Distance.why: Zero-filling a fresh table is muscle memory, and the base cases feel like empty cells rather than answers in their own right.
Edit Distance.consequence: word1 = 'abc', word2 = '': transforming a 3-character prefix into the empty string requires 3 deletions, but a zeroed column reports distance 0 — every answer built on those bases inherits the error.
Edit Distance.instead: The borders are real subproblems: turning a length-i prefix into an empty string costs exactly i deletions, so row 0 holds 0..n and column 0 holds 0..m. Fill them first and say what they mean while doing it.

Edit Distance.mistake: On mismatched characters, taking the min over insert and delete but forgetting replace.
Edit Distance.why: Insert and delete map to the two obvious table neighbors, and the diagonal reads like the matching case's private property.
Edit Distance.consequence: word1 = 'a', word2 = 'b': without replace, the cheapest route is delete plus insert for a distance of 2, but one substitution does it — the correct answer is 1.
Edit Distance.instead: Three operations, three neighbors: dp[i-1][j] is delete, dp[i][j-1] is insert, dp[i-1][j-1] is replace. Naming each neighbor with its operation out loud while writing the transition keeps all three present.

Edit Distance.mistake: Charging a cost of 1 even when the current characters match.
Edit Distance.why: Every other branch of the transition adds 1, so the plus-one gets typed on autopilot in the match branch too.
Edit Distance.consequence: word1 = 'ab', word2 = 'ab': identical strings should cost 0, but with the spurious charge the answer comes out 2 — one phantom operation per matched character.
Edit Distance.instead: A match consumes one character from both strings for free: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] with no cost term. Test on a pair of identical strings, where the only acceptable answer is 0.

Edit Distance.mistake: Writing the bare recursion over (i, j) without memoization.
Edit Distance.why: The recursive decomposition is the insight, and once it is working on small examples the caching step feels like an optimization for later.
Edit Distance.consequence: word1 = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrst', word2 = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRST' (20 characters, nothing shared): the three-way branching revisits the same (i, j) states exponentially — on the order of 3^20, about 3.5 * 10^9 calls — and times out.
Edit Distance.instead: Count the states before coding: only (i, j) matters, so there are at most (m + 1) * (n + 1) distinct subproblems. Saying the state space is m * n, so memoized time is O(m * n) is the sentence that turns the recursion into an algorithm.

Longest Common Subsequence.mistake: Solving for a common substring — requiring the shared characters to be contiguous.
Longest Common Subsequence.why: Subsequence and substring sound nearly identical, and contiguous matching is the easier mental picture to hold.
Longest Common Subsequence.consequence: s1 = 'abcde', s2 = 'ace': the longest common subsequence is 'ace' with length 3, but a contiguity-requiring scan finds only length 1 — the answer is wrong on the problem's own first example.
Longest Common Subsequence.instead: Define both terms aloud before coding: a substring is a contiguous block, a subsequence keeps relative order but may skip. Confirming which one is being asked takes five seconds and prevents solving the wrong problem entirely.

Longest Common Subsequence.mistake: Including the diagonal plus one in the mismatch branch of the transition.
Longest Common Subsequence.why: The diagonal term is on screen from the match case, and max over more options feels safer than max over fewer.
Longest Common Subsequence.consequence: s1 = 'ab', s2 = 'ba': crediting dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 on a mismatch counts a phantom match, reporting 2 where the true LCS length is 1 — either 'a' or 'b', not both in order.
Longest Common Subsequence.instead: Only equal characters may extend a common subsequence. On mismatch the transition carries forward without adding: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — the diagonal-plus-one belongs exclusively to the match branch.

Longest Common Subsequence.mistake: Letting the 1-indexed table and 0-indexed strings drift apart, comparing s1[i] against s2[j].
Longest Common Subsequence.why: dp[i][j] and s1[i] look like they name the same position, and the off-by-one only bites at the far edge of the table.
Longest Common Subsequence.consequence: s1 = 'abc', s2 = 'abc': at i = 3 the comparison reads s1[3] and crashes with an index error — or, with defensive bounds, silently compares shifted characters and returns 2 instead of 3.
Longest Common Subsequence.instead: Anchor the convention in words: dp[i][j] is the answer for the first i characters of s1 and first j of s2, so the characters under comparison are s1[i-1] and s2[j-1], always. Write the convention as a comment above the loops.

Longest Increasing Subsequence.mistake: Finding the longest contiguous increasing run instead of a subsequence.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.why: Scanning for runs is simpler and the word increasing dominates the problem name, so contiguity sneaks in unquestioned.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.consequence: nums = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]: the longest contiguous run is [3, 7, 101] with length 3, but the LIS is [2, 3, 7, 18] with length 4 — elements may be skipped.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.instead: Subsequence means keep order, skip freely, which is why each element needs a decision rather than a comparison with its neighbor. Restate the definition to the interviewer before writing any loop.

Longest Increasing Subsequence.mistake: Using <= in the comparison, letting equal elements extend the subsequence.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.why: Non-decreasing and increasing read as synonyms in a hurry, and most test arrays have distinct elements so nothing flags it.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.consequence: nums = [7, 7, 7]: with <= the answer comes out 3, but strictly increasing means the correct answer is 1 — no element can follow an equal one.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.instead: Pin the strictness with the interviewer first, then encode it: strict LIS pairs with bisect_left in the patience-sorting version, non-decreasing pairs with bisect_right. The choice of bisect function is the strictness decision in code form.

Longest Increasing Subsequence.mistake: Reporting the tails array from the O(n log n) method as the actual subsequence.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.why: The array is increasing, its length equals the LIS length, and it was built from the input, so it looks exactly like the answer.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.consequence: nums = [3, 4, 1]: the tails array finishes as [1, 4], whose elements appear in nums in the order 4 then 1 — not a valid subsequence; a real LIS is [3, 4], which shares only its length with tails.
Longest Increasing Subsequence.instead: Say what the structure means: tails[k] is the smallest value that can end an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 — bookkeeping, not a witness. To output the sequence itself, record parent pointers and reconstruct backward.

0/1 Knapsack.mistake: Optimizing to a 1-D dp array but iterating capacity from left to right.
0/1 Knapsack.why: Every other loop in the program runs left to right, and the 2-D version worked in that order, so the direction feels like a free choice.
0/1 Knapsack.consequence: weights = [2], values = [3], W = 4: left-to-right lets dp[2] = 3 feed dp[4] = dp[2] + 3 = 6 in the same item pass — the single item has been used twice; the correct answer is 3.
0/1 Knapsack.instead: Rightward iteration reads states already updated by the current item; iterating capacity from W down to the item's weight means every read comes from the previous item's row, which is exactly the 0/1 use-once guarantee compressed into one array.

0/1 Knapsack.mistake: Sorting items by value-to-weight ratio and taking greedily.
0/1 Knapsack.why: Ratio greedy is provably optimal for fractional knapsack, and the two problems are usually taught in the same breath.
0/1 Knapsack.consequence: weights = [10, 20, 30], values = [60, 100, 120], W = 50: ratio order takes the 10 and the 20 for value 160, but the optimum is the 20 and the 30 for 220 — indivisible items break the exchange argument.
0/1 Knapsack.instead: Say why greedy dies: with indivisible items you cannot top off leftover capacity with a fraction, so local ratio dominance proves nothing. The take-or-skip structure over (item, capacity) states is what remains — that is the DP.

0/1 Knapsack.mistake: Always taking an item that fits, dropping the skip branch from the transition.
0/1 Knapsack.why: If it fits and has positive value, taking it feels like it cannot hurt — the harm of occupying capacity is invisible at the moment of the choice.
0/1 Knapsack.consequence: weights = [2, 2], values = [1, 10], W = 2: forced to take the first item, capacity is spent and the answer is 1; skipping it frees the space for the second item and the correct answer is 10.
0/1 Knapsack.instead: Every item is a genuine two-way decision — dp[i][w] = max(skip, take) — because capacity spent now forecloses better items later. Write both branches explicitly, even when one looks like it could never win.

Word Break.mistake: Greedily matching the longest (or first) dictionary word at each position and never revisiting.
Word Break.why: Longest-match is how tokenizers feel like they should work, and it succeeds on most naturally worded examples.
Word Break.consequence: s = 'aaaa', wordDict = ['aaa', 'aa']: longest-first consumes 'aaa' and strands the final 'a', returning false, while 'aa' + 'aa' is a valid segmentation.
Word Break.instead: A failed split has to be able to roll back and try a shorter word — that choice structure is exactly dp[i] = any(dp[j] and s[j:i] in dict). The DP is greedy-with-undo formalized, which is why it exists.

Word Break.mistake: Writing the recursive splitter without memoization.
Word Break.why: The recursion mirrors the problem statement so directly that it feels finished once it returns correct answers on short strings.
Word Break.consequence: s = 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab' (19 a's then b), wordDict = ['a', 'aa', 'aaa']: every segmentation of the a-run is explored before each failure on the final b — an exponential number of paths for a 20-character string, and it hangs.
Word Break.instead: Notice that the only thing distinguishing recursive calls is the start index, so there are at most n + 1 distinct subproblems. Memoize on that index and the same code becomes O(n^2) with substring hashing.

Word Break.mistake: Forgetting the base case dp[0] = true, or leaving the empty prefix false.
Word Break.why: An empty string being breakable sounds like a philosophical technicality rather than load-bearing initialization.
Word Break.consequence: s = 'leetcode', wordDict = ['leet', 'code']: the check for 'leet' asks whether dp[0] is true; with dp[0] = false nothing can ever become true and the function returns false on the canonical yes-instance.
Word Break.instead: dp[0] = true encodes the zero-words-used starting state that every first word chains from. When a DP answers can it be done, ask which state represents having done nothing yet — that state must start true.

Climbing Stairs.mistake: Submitting the bare recursion f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2).
Climbing Stairs.why: The recurrence is the entire insight, and for small n the recursion returns instantly, so it feels done.
Climbing Stairs.consequence: n = 45: the call tree has on the order of fib(45), roughly 3.6 * 10^9 nodes, and the solution times out — the same subproblems are being recomputed billions of times.
Climbing Stairs.instead: Name the structure — this is Fibonacci — and collapse it to two rolling variables for O(n) time and O(1) space. Recognizing a famous recurrence by name is itself signal in an interview.

Climbing Stairs.mistake: Misaligning the base cases, seeding f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1 like textbook Fibonacci.
Climbing Stairs.why: The sequence is Fibonacci, and the textbook seed values come attached to the name.
Climbing Stairs.consequence: n = 2 should return 2 (1+1 or 2), but the textbook seed produces f(2) = 1 — every subsequent answer is shifted one position off.
Climbing Stairs.instead: Derive the bases from the problem's meaning, not the sequence's name: one way to climb one stair, two ways to climb two — or define f(0) = 1 as the one way to stand still. Verify n = 2 and n = 3 by hand before scaling up.

Climbing Stairs.mistake: Reciting the two-term recurrence in variants that allow different step sets.
Climbing Stairs.why: This problem's answer is so memorized that the recurrence feels like a property of staircases rather than of the allowed moves.
Climbing Stairs.consequence: With allowed steps {1, 2, 3} and n = 3 the answer is 4 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1, 3), but the two-term recurrence returns 3 — the memorized formula silently answers a different question.
Climbing Stairs.instead: Re-derive from the last move: f(n) = sum of f(n - s) over every allowed step s. The derivation habit is what transfers to the k-step, cost-per-stair, and skip-stair variants interviewers pivot to.

House Robber.mistake: Robbing alternating houses and returning the better of evens versus odds.
House Robber.why: No two adjacent houses compresses in the mind to every other house, and the two alternating patterns feel exhaustive.
House Robber.consequence: nums = [2, 1, 1, 9]: even indices give 2 + 1 = 3, odd give 1 + 9 = 10, but the optimum is 2 + 9 = 11 — it skips two houses in a row, which neither alternating pattern can do.
House Robber.instead: The constraint forbids adjacency; it does not mandate alternation — gaps of two or more are allowed. That extra freedom is what the recurrence best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]) explores and the patterns cannot.

House Robber.mistake: Dropping the skip branch and always robbing every second house from each position.
House Robber.why: Once best(i-2) + nums[i] is written down, it looks like the whole story — skipping the current house feels like leaving money on the table.
House Robber.consequence: nums = [1, 100, 1]: forced inclusion patterns yield 1 + 1 = 2, but the correct answer is 100 from robbing only the middle house — skipping can beat taking.
House Robber.instead: Each house is a two-way decision and the recurrence needs both arms: rob it (best(i-2) + nums[i]) or leave it (best(i-1)). The max over both is what makes the DP an argument instead of a guess.

House Robber.mistake: Seeding the second base case with nums[1] instead of the max of the first two.
House Robber.why: best(1) and nums[1] share an index, and the eye pattern-matches them as the same quantity.
House Robber.consequence: nums = [5, 1]: with best(1) = 1 the function returns 1, but the best plan for two houses is to rob the richer one — the correct answer is 5.
House Robber.instead: best(1) means the best over the first two houses, which is max(nums[0], nums[1]). Length-1 and length-2 inputs are the entire base-case surface; test both before trusting the loop.

N Queens.mistake: Checking column conflicts and one diagonal direction, forgetting the anti-diagonal.
N Queens.why: One diagonal check visually resembles the other, and boards that expose the missing direction do not show up until the search runs.
N Queens.consequence: n = 4: queens at (0, 1) and (1, 2) share the diagonal where row minus column is constant (-1 for both); with only the row-plus-column diagonal checked, the solver emits boards containing that attacking pair.
N Queens.instead: Encode each constraint as its own O(1) set: columns, row + column (one diagonal family), row - column (the other). Two queens attack diagonally exactly when they share one of those two sums — say that identity, then the check writes itself.

N Queens.mistake: Forgetting to remove the queen's marks from the sets after the recursive call returns.
N Queens.why: The add-explore rhythm feels complete on its own — undoing state after a return is not part of everyday iterative coding.
N Queens.consequence: n = 4: stale column and diagonal entries from an abandoned branch prune valid placements, and the solver reports 1 or 0 solutions where the correct count is 2.
N Queens.instead: Backtracking is a three-beat discipline — choose, explore, unchoose — and the unchoose must mirror the choose exactly, on every path including successes. Symmetric add/remove around the recursive call is the pattern to internalize.

N Queens.mistake: Appending the live mutable board to the results list at each solution.
N Queens.why: The board holds the solution at that instant, and append feels like it captures a snapshot rather than a reference.
N Queens.consequence: n = 4: both recorded entries alias the same board object, which the ongoing backtracking then mutates — the final output shows two identical fully-unwound boards instead of 2 distinct solutions.
N Queens.instead: Append a deep copy at the leaf — in Python, a fresh list of joined row strings. Aliasing a structure that backtracking will rewind is a bug family worth naming aloud; it recurs in every collect-all-solutions problem.

N Queens.mistake: Searching over all board cells — placing n queens anywhere on the n x n grid.
N Queens.why: The problem says place n queens on the board, and the direct reading of that sentence is a choice among all cells.
N Queens.consequence: n = 8: choosing 8 cells from 64 is about 4.4 * 10^9 candidate placements, versus 8! = 40320 when each row gets exactly one queen — the unstructured search times out before finding all 92 solutions.
N Queens.instead: Bake the cheapest constraint into the representation: every solution has exactly one queen per row, so let recursion depth be the row and branch only over columns. Constraints that shape the search space beat constraints that filter it afterward.

Combination Sum.mistake: Restarting the candidate loop from index 0 in every recursive call.
Combination Sum.why: Reuse is allowed, so every candidate still feels like fair game at every level of the recursion.
Combination Sum.consequence: candidates = [2, 3], target = 5: the search finds [2, 3] and [3, 2] as separate results — the same combination in two orders, which the problem counts once.
Combination Sum.instead: Pass a start index and never look left of it: reuse is expressed by recursing with the same index, not by rewinding to 0. Imposing an order on choices is the standard way to make combinations, not permutations, come out of a search.

Combination Sum.mistake: Recursing with index + 1 after taking a candidate, while intending unlimited reuse.
Combination Sum.why: Advancing the index after a choice is the habit from subset-style problems, where each element is used at most once.
Combination Sum.consequence: candidates = [2], target = 6: the only solution is [2, 2, 2], but advancing the index after the first 2 forbids reuse and the function returns an empty list.
Combination Sum.instead: The index you recurse with is the semantics: same index means may take this candidate again, index + 1 means done with it forever. Point at that argument and say which meaning you intend — it is the whole difference from Combination Sum II.

Combination Sum.mistake: Appending the shared path list to results at the base case without copying.
Combination Sum.why: At the moment of success the path holds exactly the right elements, and append reads like it stores those values.
Combination Sum.consequence: candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7: the stored references all point at the one live path list, which backtracking then pops — the output shows empty or garbled lists instead of [2, 2, 3] and [7].
Combination Sum.instead: Store a snapshot: append list(path) when target reaches 0. The pop that follows every recursive call is the same list being rewound — results must be immune to it.

Reverse Linked List.mistake: Rewiring curr.next to prev before saving the rest of the list.
Reverse Linked List.why: The reversal is the point of the exercise, so the pointer flip feels like the first thing each iteration should do.
Reverse Linked List.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3: flipping node 1's pointer first orphans nodes 2 and 3 — the walk has nowhere to go after one step and the function returns a 1-node list.
Reverse Linked List.instead: The three-step order is load-bearing: save next = curr.next, then flip curr.next = prev, then advance both. Keep the invariant in words — prev heads the fully reversed prefix, curr heads the untouched suffix — and the order becomes hard to get wrong.

Reverse Linked List.mistake: Returning the original head pointer after the loop finishes.
Reverse Linked List.why: head has meant the answer for the whole function, and returning it is pure habit.
Reverse Linked List.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3: the old head node 1 is now the tail with a null next pointer, so the caller receives a 1-element list instead of 3 -> 2 -> 1.
Reverse Linked List.instead: When the loop ends, curr has walked off the end and prev rests on the last node processed — the new head. Returning prev is the correct move, and explaining why is a two-second credibility win.

Reverse Linked List.mistake: In the recursive version, setting head.next.next = head but never clearing head.next.
Reverse Linked List.why: The forward flip is the clever line everyone remembers; the cleanup line looks optional next to it.
Reverse Linked List.consequence: list 1 -> 2: after the flip, node 2 points to node 1 and node 1 still points to node 2 — a 2-node cycle, and any traversal or print of the result loops forever.
Reverse Linked List.instead: Sever the old forward edge with head.next = None immediately after the flip; the recursion's contract is that head becomes a tail. Verify the 2-node list by hand — it is the smallest input that exposes the cycle.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.mistake: Detecting a revisit by comparing node values.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.why: Seen this value before is the natural reading of revisiting, and on lists with distinct values it even works.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.consequence: list 1 -> 1 -> 1 built from three distinct nodes with no cycle: value comparison reports a repeat at the second node and declares a cycle that does not exist.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.instead: A cycle is about identity, not content — the same node object reached twice. Hash node references (not values), or avoid storage entirely with Floyd's slow and fast pointers meeting inside the loop.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.mistake: Advancing the fast pointer two steps without null-checking both fast and fast.next.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.why: The loop's mental model is about the cycle case, where nothing is ever null, so the acyclic exit path gets no attention.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.consequence: acyclic list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: fast reaches the end and the next double-step dereferences null — a crash on exactly the boring input that should return false.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.instead: Make the loop condition carry the acyclic case: while fast and fast.next. A cycle announces itself by the meeting; the absence of a cycle announces itself by fast falling off the end — both exits deserve code.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.mistake: Comparing slow and fast before either pointer has moved.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.why: Initialize, then loop while different reads naturally, and both pointers start at the head together.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.consequence: any list, e.g. acyclic 1 -> 2: slow and fast are equal at step 0, so the pre-check loop reports a cycle immediately on every input.
Detect Cycle in Linked List.instead: Move first, compare after — a do-while shape — or offset the start with fast = head.next and account for it. The meeting is only evidence of a cycle when it happens after movement.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Looping while both lists are non-empty and dropping whatever remains.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.why: The interleaving loop is where the thinking happens, so when it ends the merge feels finished.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: l1 = 1 -> 3, l2 = 2 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6: the loop ends when l1 empties, and the output 1 -> 2 -> 3 silently loses 4 -> 5 -> 6.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.instead: The leftover run is already sorted and already linked, so attach it whole with one assignment: tail.next = l1 or l2. Recognizing that the remainder needs no per-node work is part of the expected answer.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Managing the head of the result without a dummy node, branching on which list starts.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.why: A placeholder node feels like a wasteful trick, and handling the first element specially seems more honest.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: l1 = None, l2 = 1 -> 2: the head-selection branches multiply — empty inputs, equal firsts — and one missed branch returns None or crashes on exactly the empty-list edge case.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.instead: A dummy head (a throwaway node whose next will be the answer) makes the first attachment identical to every other attachment, deleting the special cases wholesale. Return dummy.next and mention why the trick exists — uniformity, not cleverness.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Writing the elegant recursive merge without considering stack depth.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.why: The recursive version is four lines, reads like the definition, and every tutorial shows it.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: two lists of 10^5 nodes each: recursion depth reaches 2 * 10^5, far past Python's default limit near 1000 — RecursionError on large inputs that the iterative version handles without effort.
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.instead: Match the tool to the input bound: recursion depth here is O(m + n), so quote the constraint and choose the iterative tail-pointer version when lists can be long. Naming the depth limit before it bites is the senior move.

Remove Nth Node From End.mistake: Counting the length, then walking to the target node itself instead of its predecessor.
Remove Nth Node From End.why: The problem says remove the nth node, so the walk naturally aims at the node being removed.
Remove Nth Node From End.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, n = 2: the target is node 4, but standing on node 4 you cannot unlink it — you need node 3 to redirect its next pointer, and code that stops on 4 deletes the wrong link.
Remove Nth Node From End.instead: Deletion in a singly linked list is an operation on the predecessor, so aim the walk at position length - n counting from a dummy node before the head. Framing every deletion as find the predecessor removes the off-by-one.

Remove Nth Node From End.mistake: Running the one-pass two-pointer gap trick starting from the real head.
Remove Nth Node From End.why: The head is where every traversal starts, and the gap arithmetic looks self-contained.
Remove Nth Node From End.consequence: list 1 -> 2, n = 2: the node to delete is the head itself; with both pointers started at head, slow ends on the head rather than before it, and there is no predecessor to rewire — wrong deletion or a crash, where the expected output is the list [2].
Remove Nth Node From End.instead: Start both pointers at a dummy node in front of the head and advance fast n + 1 steps; slow then lands on the predecessor in every case, including head deletion. The dummy exists precisely to give the head a predecessor.

Remove Nth Node From End.mistake: Leaving the relationship between n and the list length unexamined.
Remove Nth Node From End.why: The judge's constraints quietly guarantee validity, so the boundary never surfaces during practice.
Remove Nth Node From End.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3 with n = 3 is in range — it deletes the head, and code without a dummy breaks on it; if n could exceed the length, the fast pointer walks off the end and dereferences null.
Remove Nth Node From End.instead: State the assumption aloud — the standard guarantee is 1 <= n <= length — and observe that the extreme in-range case, deleting the head, must still work. Explicitly testing the boundary the constraints allow is what separates careful from lucky.

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.mistake: Ending the loop when both lists are exhausted, discarding a final carry.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.why: No digits left feels synonymous with nothing left to do, and most test cases end carry-free.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.consequence: l1 = 5, l2 = 5: the digit sum is 10, producing digit 0 with carry 1, but the loop exits and the output is the single node 0 instead of 0 -> 1.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.instead: Make carry a first-class loop participant: continue while l1 or l2 or carry is non-zero. The final carry is not cleanup — it is one more digit the answer owes you.

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.mistake: Converting both lists to integers, adding, and converting back.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.why: The lists represent numbers, and the language already knows how to add numbers, so the detour through arithmetic feels like engineering sense.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.consequence: a 20-node list encodes a 20-digit number, which overflows a 64-bit integer (max about 9.2 * 10^18, only 19 digits) in Java or C++; Python hides the overflow but the interviewer wanted the digit-wise algorithm, not a language loophole.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.instead: Add digit by digit with a carry, the way column addition works on paper — the linked structure is the point of the problem. Mention the overflow bound explicitly; knowing where 64 bits run out is part of the answer.

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.mistake: Stopping the addition at the end of the shorter list.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.why: Pairwise addition needs two operands, so the loop over pairs feels like it should end when pairs run out.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.consequence: l1 = 9 -> 9, l2 = 1 (99 + 1): stopping at the shorter list emits 0 -> something and never produces the third digit — the correct output is 0 -> 0 -> 1, which is 100.
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.instead: Treat a missing node as digit 0 and keep the loop running while any list or the carry remains. Uneven lengths are not an edge case to patch; they are the normal case the loop shape must absorb.

Reverse Nodes in K Group.mistake: Reversing the final partial group along with the full ones.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.why: The reversal machinery is already running, and letting it finish the tail feels more uniform than special-casing it.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 with k = 3: the correct output is 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5, but reversing the leftover pair produces 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 5 -> 4 — the spec says a group shorter than k stays as-is.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.instead: Probe before you commit: walk a scout pointer k steps ahead, and only reverse when a full group is confirmed. The check-then-act split is what keeps the tail intact.

Reverse Nodes in K Group.mistake: Reversing each group correctly but botching the reconnection between groups.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.why: The reversal is the hard-looking part, so attention pools there and the two boundary links feel like bookkeeping.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 with k = 2: the groups become 2 -> 1 and 4 -> 3, but node 1 still points at node 2 from before the reversal — traversal revisits nodes in a loop or loses 4 -> 3 entirely.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.instead: Name three handles per group before touching pointers: the previous group's tail, this group's head (which becomes its tail), and this group's tail (which becomes its head). Rewire both boundary links after each reversal, with a dummy node in front of the first group.

Reverse Nodes in K Group.mistake: Counting the group with a loop that runs one node too far, or dereferencing past the end while counting.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.why: Count k nodes and check k nodes ahead differ by one in every implementation, and the difference only bites at the list's end.
Reverse Nodes in K Group.consequence: list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 with k = 5: an overshooting count loop asks for node 6, reads null, and either crashes or wrongly concludes the group is short — leaving the list unreversed when the correct output is 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1.
