Reverse Nodes in K Group.instead: Advance a scout exactly k times with a null check at each step, and bail to append-as-is the moment it runs out early. Verify on a list whose length is an exact multiple of k, where the last group must still reverse.

Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.mistake: Copying random pointers directly, so clone nodes point into the original list.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.why: copy.random = old.random type-checks, runs, and even makes the values traversal look right, so nothing appears wrong.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.consequence: nodes [[7, null], [13, 0]]: the cloned 13's random points at the original 7, not the cloned 7 — the judge's independence check fails, and any later mutation of the original corrupts the so-called copy.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.instead: The random targets may not exist yet when you copy a node, so build in two passes with an old-to-new map: create all clone nodes first, then wire every next and random by translating through the map.

Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.mistake: Using the O(1)-space interleaving trick but never un-weaving the two lists at the end.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.why: Once the clone's randoms are wired, the answer exists, and the separation pass feels like cosmetic cleanup.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.consequence: nodes [[3, null], [3, 0], [3, null]]: the original list is left interleaved with clone nodes (A -> A' -> B -> B' ...), and the judge — which verifies the original is unmodified — rejects the submission outright.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.instead: The trick is a three-pass contract: interleave clones after originals, set copy.random = orig.random.next, then restore both lists to their own chains. Leaving inputs as you found them is part of correctness, not politeness.

Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.mistake: Keying the old-to-new map by node value instead of node identity.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.why: Values are what you see when debugging, and dictionaries keyed by values are the everyday pattern.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.consequence: nodes [[1, null], [1, 0]]: two distinct nodes share value 1, the map collapses them into one entry, and the clone comes out with merged or misdirected pointers.
Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.instead: Identity is the node reference itself — values are payload and may repeat freely. Key the map by the node object (its reference), which is exactly what makes the translation old node to its clone well-defined.

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Merging list 1 into list 2, the result into list 3, and so on down the line.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.why: Two-list merge is a solved subroutine, and folding the lists through it one at a time is the most direct way to reuse it.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: k = 10^4 lists totaling N = 10^5 nodes: early nodes are re-traversed in nearly every later merge, and the O(k * N) total approaches 10^9 operations — a timeout where O(N log k) passes comfortably.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.instead: Keep every merge between similarly sized inputs: pair the lists up and merge halves (divide and conquer), or draw the global minimum repeatedly from a min-heap of the k current heads. Both make each node travel only log k merges.

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Pushing bare list nodes into Python's heapq with no tiebreaker.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.why: The heap needs the smallest value first, and pushing (node.val, node) or the node itself looks like it hands the heap what it needs.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: lists = [[1, 4], [1, 3]]: two nodes tie on value 1, heapq falls through to comparing ListNode objects, and the program dies with TypeError: '<' not supported between instances.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.instead: Give ties a total order the heap can use: push (val, seq, node) where seq is a rising counter. The middle element never affects which value wins — it exists to keep the comparison from ever reaching the node object.

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.mistake: Seeding the heap with every list head, including the empty ones.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.why: The lists arrive as a uniform array, and a uniform loop over them feels like the natural setup step.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.consequence: lists = [[], [1], []]: pushing None for the empty lists crashes on the first attribute access (None.val), or poisons every heap comparison — on an input the judge is guaranteed to include.
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.instead: Guard both entry points: push only non-null heads at setup, and only a non-null successor after each pop. Empty lists among the k inputs are the first edge case this problem tests.

LRU Cache.mistake: Treating get() as a pure read that does not touch recency order.
LRU Cache.why: In every ordinary map, reading is side-effect-free, and mutating state inside a getter feels like a design smell.
LRU Cache.consequence: capacity 2: put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3) — the eviction must remove key 2, but without the recency refresh key 1 is evicted, and a later get(1) returns -1 instead of 1.
LRU Cache.instead: Recently used includes reads — that is the R in LRU. Both get and put must move the touched key to the most-recent position; the cache is an ordering structure that happens to store values.

LRU Cache.mistake: Running the eviction check before checking whether the key already exists.
LRU Cache.why: Capacity is the scary constraint, so guarding it first feels like defensive programming.
LRU Cache.consequence: capacity 2: put(1, 1), put(2, 2), put(2, 20) — the overwrite adds no new key, but evict-first removes least-recent key 1 anyway, and a later get(1) returns -1 where it should return 1.
LRU Cache.instead: An update in place never changes the size, so the order is: if the key exists, update its value and refresh recency, done; only a genuinely new key at full capacity triggers eviction. State the order of operations before coding put.

LRU Cache.mistake: One hash map with timestamps, scanning for the oldest entry at eviction time.
LRU Cache.why: It needs no second data structure, and the timestamp scan is easy to write correctly on the first try.
LRU Cache.consequence: 10^5 operations at capacity 10^4: each eviction scans the whole map, and the worst case approaches 10^9 comparisons — the problem's O(1)-per-operation requirement is the actual exercise.
LRU Cache.instead: Pair the hash map with a doubly linked list ordered by recency: the map finds the node in O(1), the list moves and evicts in O(1). Explain why singly linked fails — removing an arbitrary node in O(1) requires its predecessor pointer — and mention OrderedDict or LinkedHashMap as the packaged form.

LRU Cache.mistake: Writing the doubly linked list with real head and tail nodes instead of permanent sentinels.
LRU Cache.why: Dummy nodes feel like clutter, and the pointer surgery seems manageable while the list is on the whiteboard.
LRU Cache.consequence: capacity 1: put(1, 1), put(2, 2) — the very first eviction removes the only real node, hitting the head-and-tail-both-change branch; one missed null check crashes the cache on its simplest workload.
LRU Cache.instead: Permanent dummy head and tail sentinels guarantee every real node has live neighbors, collapsing insert and remove to branch-free pointer swaps. Buying uniformity with two throwaway nodes is the standard trade — take it every time.

Min Stack.mistake: Tracking the minimum in a single variable alongside the stack.
Min Stack.why: Running minimum of what I have pushed is one value, and one variable is the natural home for one value.
Min Stack.consequence: push(1), push(0), pop(): the variable still says 0, but 0 has left the stack — getMin() now returns 0 while the true minimum of the remaining contents is 1.
Min Stack.instead: Pops must be able to restore the previous minimum, so the history of minimums has to be stored, not summarized: keep an auxiliary stack of minimums (or push value-minimum pairs) that moves in lockstep with the main stack.

Min Stack.mistake: Pushing onto the auxiliary min-stack only when the new value is strictly smaller than the current minimum.
Min Stack.why: An equal value does not change the minimum, so recording it again feels like storing redundant information.
Min Stack.consequence: push(0), push(0), pop(): the aux stack recorded 0 once; the pop sees the departing 0 matching the aux top and removes it, leaving the aux empty while a 0 still sits in the stack — getMin() is now wrong or crashes.
Min Stack.instead: Duplicates of the minimum each need their own aux entry, because each will eventually be popped: push on less-than-or-equal, or sidestep the whole class of bug by pushing to the aux stack on every operation.

Min Stack.mistake: Implementing getMin() as a scan over the stack contents.
Min Stack.why: It is correct, requires no extra structure, and feels acceptable for a supporting operation.
Min Stack.consequence: 10^5 getMin calls against a stack holding 10^5 elements approach 10^10 comparisons — and the problem statement demands O(1) for every operation, which is the entire reason this problem exists.
Min Stack.instead: Spend O(1) extra memory per push to make the answer instantaneous: the aux-stack top always is the minimum. Name the trade — space for time — and mention the delta-encoding variant that gets O(1) extra space if the follow-up asks.

Balanced Parentheses.mistake: Keeping one counter per bracket type and checking that all end at zero.
Balanced Parentheses.why: Balanced sounds like a counting property — equal opens and closes — and counters implement counting directly.
Balanced Parentheses.consequence: s = '([)]': every counter finishes at 0, so the counters say valid, but the interleaving is illegal — the correct answer is false because the parenthesis closes while the bracket is still open.
Balanced Parentheses.instead: Validity is about order, not totals: the most recently opened bracket must close first, which is a last-in-first-out constraint. That sentence is the justification for a stack — push openers, and each closer must match the popped top.

Balanced Parentheses.mistake: Popping for a closer without first checking that the stack is non-empty.
Balanced Parentheses.why: The mental movie always starts with an opener, so the closer-first script never gets rehearsed.
Balanced Parentheses.consequence: s = ')(': the first character is a closer with nothing open, the pop hits an empty stack, and the function dies with an exception instead of returning false.
Balanced Parentheses.instead: A closer arriving at an empty stack is not an error condition — it is the answer: return false immediately. Put the emptiness check before the pop and treat it as a normal exit path.

Balanced Parentheses.mistake: Returning true as soon as the scan completes without inspecting the stack.
Balanced Parentheses.why: Surviving the whole string without a mismatch feels like passing every test the input could pose.
Balanced Parentheses.consequence: s = '(((': the loop finishes without conflict, but three openers were never closed — the function returns true where the correct answer is false.
Balanced Parentheses.instead: The scan proves no closer mismatched; it says nothing about openers still waiting. Valid means everything opened was closed, so the final answer is whether the stack is empty — return stack.isEmpty(), not true.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.mistake: For every bar, expanding left and right to find how far its height stretches.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.why: It is the geometric definition of the answer restated as code, and it works instantly on the samples.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.consequence: heights = [1] * 100000 (all equal): every expansion runs the full width of the array, the total is O(n^2) at around 10^10 steps, and the submission times out.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.instead: The question for each bar is where is the first shorter bar on each side, and a monotonic stack — a stack kept in increasing height order — answers it for all bars in one pass, each index pushed and popped once.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.mistake: Computing the popped bar's width from its own index instead of the stack's new top.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.why: The popped bar is the star of the calculation, so its index feels like the natural anchor for the span.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.consequence: heights = [2, 1, 2]: the true answer is 3 — height 1 spanning all three bars — but anchoring widths to popped indices undercounts the stretch across the popped region and yields 2.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.instead: After popping, the bar's reach spans strictly between the new stack top and the current index: width = i - stack.top - 1, or i when the stack empties. The popped bar extends over bars taller than it that were popped earlier — the new top is the real left boundary.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.mistake: Ending the scan without draining the bars still on the stack.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.why: The pop-and-measure logic lives inside the main loop, so when the input ends the algorithm appears to be finished.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.consequence: heights = [1, 2, 3]: strictly increasing bars never trigger a pop during the scan, nothing is ever measured, and the function returns 0 instead of 4 (height 2 across the last two bars).
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.instead: Bars still stacked at the end extend to the array's right edge and must be measured: append a sentinel bar of height 0 to force the pops, or run the identical pop logic once more with i = n. The drain is not cleanup — it is where increasing inputs get their entire answer.

Sliding Window Maximum.mistake: Calling max() on the window slice at every step.
Sliding Window Maximum.why: It is one readable line, and for the sample sizes in the prompt it returns instantly.
Sliding Window Maximum.consequence: nums of length 10^5 with k = 5 * 10^4: each of the ~10^5 windows scans up to 5 * 10^4 elements, about 5 * 10^9 operations total — a guaranteed timeout on the stated constraints.
Sliding Window Maximum.instead: Successive windows share almost all their elements, so the work must be shared too: a monotonic deque (a double-ended queue of indices whose values decrease front to back) gives amortized O(1) per element, O(n) total.

Sliding Window Maximum.mistake: Expiring the front of the deque unconditionally on every slide.
Sliding Window Maximum.why: The window moves by one each step, so removing one thing from the deque each step feels like the matching motion.
Sliding Window Maximum.consequence: nums = [1, 3, 2], k = 2: after the first window the deque holds only index 1 (value 3, since 1 was dominated); sliding to window [3, 2] unconditionally evicts 3, and the reported max becomes 2 instead of 3.
Sliding Window Maximum.instead: The deque is a list of still-useful candidates, not a mirror of the window — it shrinks from the front only when the front's index has actually left the window. Store indices, and expire the front exactly when it equals i - k.

Sliding Window Maximum.mistake: Maintaining the deque in increasing order, or popping dominated elements from the wrong end.
Sliding Window Maximum.why: Sorted ascending is the default mental picture of an ordered structure, and either end of a deque will accept the pop.
Sliding Window Maximum.consequence: nums = [3, 1, 2], k = 3: with an increasing deque the front holds the minimum, and the reported answer for the window is 1 instead of 3.
Sliding Window Maximum.instead: State the invariant before coding: values decrease from front to back, the front is the current maximum, and a new element evicts smaller elements from the back because they can never outrank it while it remains — dominated is the word that keeps the direction straight.

Kth Largest Element.mistake: Sorting the whole array and indexing from the end, with nothing further to say.
Kth Largest Element.why: It is three characters of thought, unquestionably correct, and interview nerves reward the safe move.
Kth Largest Element.consequence: Nothing fails on nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2 — but the interviewer's follow-ups (n = 10^6 with k = 10, then a streaming version) are the actual assessment, and full sorting at O(n log n) answers neither.
Kth Largest Element.instead: Lay out the ladder yourself: sort is O(n log n), a size-k min-heap is O(n log k) and handles streams, quickselect averages O(n) on static arrays. Choosing per constraints — and asking about duplicates and data volume — is the answer.

Kth Largest Element.mistake: Keeping a size-k max-heap and evicting the largest element when it overflows.
Kth Largest Element.why: The problem says largest, so a max-heap feels like the aligned tool, and eviction from the top is the only eviction a heap offers.
Kth Largest Element.consequence: nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2: evicting the maximum repeatedly leaves the two smallest values [1, 2] in the heap, and the function returns 2 — the correct answer is 5.
Kth Largest Element.instead: To retain the k largest, throw away the smallest of the current candidates — which means a min-heap of size k, whose root is exactly the kth largest at the end. Which element must be cheap to discard decides the heap's polarity.

Kth Largest Element.mistake: Deduplicating the array, or otherwise conflating kth largest with kth distinct value.
Kth Largest Element.why: In everyday speech the second largest of [5, 5, 3] is 3, so removing duplicates feels like fidelity to the question.
Kth Largest Element.consequence: nums = [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4: the standard problem counts duplicates and the answer is 4; a dedupe-first solution returns 3 and fails the judge.
Kth Largest Element.instead: This is a specification fork, so resolve it with one clarifying sentence before coding — the standard version ranks with duplicates counted. Asking is free; guessing costs the whole solution.

Top K Frequent Elements.mistake: Counting frequencies, then sorting all entries by count.
Top K Frequent Elements.why: Count then sort by count is the natural two-step reading of the problem title, and it is correct.
Top K Frequent Elements.consequence: Nothing fails on nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2 — but the stated follow-up requires better than O(n log n), and with n = 10^6 distinct-heavy data the full sort is exactly what was ruled out.
Top K Frequent Elements.instead: Frequencies live in a tiny range — no count can exceed n — so bucket them: an array of lists indexed by count, walked from the high end until k elements are collected. Bounded key ranges are the standing invitation to replace sorting with indexing.

Top K Frequent Elements.mistake: Building heap entries with the element first, so the heap orders by element value instead of by count.
Top K Frequent Elements.why: (element, count) is the order the data appears in the counter, and tuples flow into the heap without complaint.
Top K Frequent Elements.consequence: nums = [5, 5, 5, 1, 1, 4], k = 2: the expected answer is [5, 1] (counts 3 and 2), but a size-2 min-heap ordered by element value evicts the small elements and returns [4, 5].
Top K Frequent Elements.instead: A heap compares tuples left to right, so the sort key must come first: push (count, element). Whenever a heap of tuples misbehaves, the first suspect is which field is doing the comparing.

Top K Frequent Elements.mistake: In the bucket version, storing one element per frequency slot instead of a list.
Top K Frequent Elements.why: Frequency feels like a unique label per element, and a flat array of single slots is less code than an array of lists.
Top K Frequent Elements.consequence: nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2: elements 1 and 2 both have frequency 2; a single-slot bucket keeps only one of them, and the returned pair is missing a correct element or includes 3.
Top K Frequent Elements.instead: Frequencies collide — many elements can share one count — so each bucket must hold a list. Walk buckets from frequency n downward, extending the result until it reaches k elements.

Find Median from Data Stream.mistake: Keeping a sorted list and inserting each arrival with binary-search insort.
Find Median from Data Stream.why: bisect finds the position in O(log n), and the log is what sticks in memory as the cost of the operation.
Find Median from Data Stream.consequence: 10^5 addNum calls: the binary search is O(log n) but each insertion shifts O(n) elements, so the total approaches 5 * 10^9 element moves — the insert's hidden linear cost is what times out.
Find Median from Data Stream.instead: The median only ever needs the boundary between the lower and upper halves, so keep exactly that boundary: a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half. Insert is O(log n) for real, and the median reads off the roots in O(1).

Find Median from Data Stream.mistake: Routing each arrival into a heap by comparison alone, without rebalancing sizes.
Find Median from Data Stream.why: Small values go low, large values go high sounds like the complete sorting rule, and early streams keep the sizes close by luck.
Find Median from Data Stream.consequence: stream 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 routed by comparison against the low half's max: the low heap keeps [1] while the high heap grows to [2, 3, 4, 5], and findMedian reports 1.5 instead of 3.
Find Median from Data Stream.instead: The heaps' size gap is the invariant that makes the roots the median — after every insert, restore abs(len(low) - len(high)) <= 1 by moving one root across. Route by comparison, then rebalance by size, every single time.

Find Median from Data Stream.mistake: Scattering Python's negation-based max-heap workaround across the code.
Find Median from Data Stream.why: heapq only provides a min-heap, and negating on push is the well-known workaround, so each call site gets patched where it stands.
Find Median from Data Stream.consequence: stream 5, 2: the low half stores -5 internally; one read that forgets to negate reports a median of -5 or -3.5 instead of 3.5 — a sign bug invisible until a test checks actual values.
Find Median from Data Stream.instead: Confine the negation to one place: tiny helpers like pushLow(x) doing heappush(low, -x) and peekLow() returning -low[0]. When a data structure needs an encoding trick, wrap the trick so the rest of the code never sees it.

Level Order Traversal.mistake: Draining one queue in a single loop without recording where each level ends.
Level Order Traversal.why: BFS is remembered as one queue, one loop, and the traversal order does come out correct — only the grouping is lost.
Level Order Traversal.consequence: tree [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: the output is the flat list [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] instead of the required [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]] — right order, wrong shape, judged wrong.
Level Order Traversal.instead: The queue holds exactly one level at the top of each outer iteration, so snapshot size = len(queue) and drain precisely that many nodes into the current level's list before their children take over the queue.

Level Order Traversal.mistake: Enqueueing null children and planning to filter them on the way out.
Level Order Traversal.why: Pushing whatever left and right contain keeps the enqueue line short, and the nulls feel handleable later.
Level Order Traversal.consequence: tree [1, null, 2]: the null left child enters the queue and the dequeue side either crashes reading .val on None or pollutes the level lists with placeholder entries.
Level Order Traversal.instead: Filter at the entrance, not the exit: enqueue a child only if it is non-null. The queue's invariant — every element is a real node — is worth one if-statement per child, and it deletes the entire downstream null-handling story.

Level Order Traversal.mistake: In the recursive depth-tagged version, appending to result[depth] before that sublist exists.
Level Order Traversal.why: The recursion carries depth as an argument, and indexing result by it reads like the sublist should already be there.
Level Order Traversal.consequence: tree [1, 2, 3]: the first visit at depth 1 executes result[1].append(...) while result has length 1 — an IndexError on a three-node tree.
Level Order Traversal.instead: Create-on-first-visit: when depth == len(result), append an empty list before writing into it. Or side-step the bookkeeping entirely with BFS, whose loop structure matches the output shape level by level.

Diameter of Binary Tree.mistake: Computing left depth plus right depth at the root only.
Diameter of Binary Tree.why: The longest path in the examples usually does run through the root, and the root is where the recursion naturally reports.
Diameter of Binary Tree.consequence: tree [1, 2, null, 3, 4, 5, null, null, 6] — root 1 has only a left child 2, whose subtree holds the path 5 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 6 of length 4; measuring at the root alone gives 3.
Diameter of Binary Tree.instead: The best path bends at some node, but not necessarily the root, so evaluate leftDepth + rightDepth at every node during one post-order pass, tracking the running best while returning depth to the parent.

Diameter of Binary Tree.mistake: Counting nodes on the path instead of edges.
Diameter of Binary Tree.why: Length of a path colloquially means how many things are on it, and both conventions produce plausible-looking numbers.
Diameter of Binary Tree.consequence: tree [1, 2, 3]: the diameter in edges is 2, but a node-count answer says 3 — every answer is off by one against the judge's convention.
Diameter of Binary Tree.instead: Pin the unit before writing the recursion: the standard problem counts edges, so a single node has diameter 0. Deciding the convention first also settles what a leaf's depth is, which is where the off-by-ones breed.

Diameter of Binary Tree.mistake: Calling a standalone depth() helper for both children of every node.
Diameter of Binary Tree.why: Depth is already written and diameter is defined in terms of it, so composing the two functions feels like clean reuse.
Diameter of Binary Tree.consequence: a skewed, linked-list-shaped tree with 10^4 nodes: each of the n nodes pays an O(n) depth call, the total is about 10^8, and the clean-looking solution times out.
Diameter of Binary Tree.instead: Fuse the two computations: one post-order traversal returns depth upward while updating a shared best diameter as a side effect. The return one value, record another pattern reappears across tree problems — this is the one to learn it on.

Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.mistake: Returning the forked sum — node plus both children's gains — up to the parent.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.why: The fork is the quantity being maximized, so returning it feels like passing the good news upward.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [2, 1, null, 3, 4]: node 1 forks over both leaves for 3 + 1 + 4 = 8; handing 8 to node 2 claims the path 3 -> 1 -> 4 -> 2, which revisits node 1 — an illegal path scoring 10 where the true best is 8.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.instead: Track two different quantities: the forked sum through a node feeds only the global best, while the value returned to the parent is node plus one child arm — a path continuing upward cannot have already branched.

Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.mistake: Adding a child's contribution even when that contribution is negative.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.why: The recursion hands back a number per child, and the formula consumes both numbers — declining one does not occur to the formula.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [2, -1]: forcing the -1 branch into the path gives 1, but the best path is the bare node 2 — a path may exclude a subtree entirely.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.instead: Clamp each child's gain at zero: gain = max(0, childGain). The clamp is the code-level expression of paths are allowed to leave losing branches out, and it belongs in the recursion, not in post-processing.

Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.why: Zero is the reflexive identity for a maximum-of-sums, and it is right whenever any node is positive.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [-3]: the single node is the only possible path and the answer is -3, but a zero-initialized best returns 0 — the sum of an empty path the problem forbids.
Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree.instead: The path must contain at least one node, so start best at negative infinity (or the root's value) and let real paths compete from there. Whenever a problem forbids the empty case, an identity-element initialization is the first thing to re-examine.

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.mistake: Steering the search by comparing node values, as in the BST version.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.why: The BST variant is usually learned first, and its value-comparison walk is shorter and feels like the general technique.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8], p = 5, q = 1: values carry no ordering information in a plain binary tree, so the comparisons steer arbitrarily — the walk misses the answer 3 or descends nowhere useful.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.instead: Without ordering, both subtrees must be asked: recurse left and right for sightings of p or q. A node where both sides report a sighting is the split point — the LCA. Note explicitly that the BST shortcut was a property of the structure, not of the problem.

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.mistake: Requiring the split — non-null reports from both children — as the only way to answer.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.why: The split point is the memorable picture of an LCA, so the ancestor-of-the-other case slips out of the mental model.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [3, 5, 1, 6, 2], p = 5, q = 2: q lives inside p's subtree, so no node sees a split — the expected answer is 5 itself, and split-only logic returns 3 or null.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.instead: A node counts as its own ancestor, so the recursion returns root immediately when root matches p or q — the guarantee that both nodes exist makes stopping there sound, since the other node must be below or elsewhere. State that reliance on the guarantee aloud.

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.mistake: Collecting both root-to-node paths and comparing them, without handling absence.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.why: Two paths diverging at the LCA is a very visual, very checkable plan, and it does work when both nodes exist.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.consequence: tree [1, 2], p = 3, q = 2 in the variant where nodes may be absent: the path to 3 comes back empty, and the comparison loop crowns a bogus ancestor from comparing against an empty list — plus the approach costs two traversals and O(n) extra space.
Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.instead: Say which contract you are coding against: with existence guaranteed, the one-pass recursion needs no absence handling; without it, count found nodes and verify both were seen. The follow-up about missing nodes is a standard second act for this problem.

Validate BST.mistake: Checking each node only against its immediate children.
Validate BST.why: The BST rule is usually recited as left child smaller, right child bigger, which is a parent-child sentence.
Validate BST.consequence: tree [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20]: every parent-child pair passes (15 > 10, 6 < 15, 20 > 15), yet 6 sits in 10's right subtree while being smaller than 10 — the tree is invalid and the local check approves it.
Validate BST.instead: The BST property is a subtree-wide constraint: every node bounds all descendants on each side. Thread an allowed range (low, high) down the recursion, tightening one bound at each turn — the range is the property, made explicit.

Validate BST.mistake: Seeding the valid range with fixed integer limits like INT_MIN and INT_MAX.
Validate BST.why: They read as the widest possible bounds, and on ordinary inputs nothing ever touches them.
Validate BST.consequence: single-node tree [2147483647]: the node equals INT_MAX, the strict check value < high fails against the seed bound, and a valid tree is rejected.
Validate BST.instead: Make the initial bounds mean no constraint rather than a large number: null sentinels or infinities, or a long-typed bound. Better still, validate via inorder order — each visited value must exceed its predecessor — and the seed-bound problem disappears.

Validate BST.mistake: Allowing equal values by validating with less-than-or-equal.
Validate BST.why: Real-world databases store duplicates, so equality feels like it should be tolerated somewhere in the tree.
Validate BST.consequence: tree [2, 2, 2]: the standard definition requires strict inequality on both sides, so this tree is invalid — the lenient check returns true and fails the judge.
Validate BST.instead: Duplicates policy is a specification question: ask, then encode the answer deliberately. The default convention is strict — left subtree strictly smaller, right strictly larger — and mixing conventions mid-recursion is the bug to guard against.

Validate BST.mistake: Comparing inorder values against a previous variable initialized to 0.
Validate BST.why: Zero is the default initial value the fingers type, and trees full of positive values never expose it.
Validate BST.consequence: tree [-5, -10, 0] (inorder -10, -5, 0, a valid BST): the first comparison sees -10 < 0 with the seed previous of 0 and declares the tree invalid.
Validate BST.instead: The state before any node is visited is no predecessor yet, and the code should say so: previous = None with a first-visit branch, or negative infinity. Defaults that accidentally lie about state are a bug class, not a style choice.

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.mistake: Serializing plain preorder without markers for the null children.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.why: Preorder feels like it captures the tree — it visits everything — and nulls look like absent data not worth writing down.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.consequence: the tree [1, 2] (2 as left child) and the tree [1, null, 2] (2 as right child) both serialize to '1,2' — deserialization cannot tell them apart, so one of them round-trips into the wrong shape.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.instead: Record the nulls: '1,2,#,#,#' pins every child slot. With null markers, a single preorder stream determines the tree uniquely, and deserialization becomes one recursive read with no lookahead.

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.mistake: Reconstructing from a preorder-plus-inorder pair of traversals.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.why: It is the famous construct-a-tree technique from another classic problem, so it feels like the designed tool for round-tripping.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.consequence: a tree whose root 3 has a child also valued 3: preorder [3, 3] with inorder [3, 3] cannot distinguish left child from right — position-by-value lookup is ambiguous the moment values repeat.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.instead: That technique assumes distinct values, which a serializer cannot assume. Null-marked preorder encodes structure explicitly instead of inferring it from value positions, so duplicates cost nothing — prefer encodings that never need to search.

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.mistake: Deserializing recursively while passing the read position as a plain integer argument.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.why: Recursion communicates through arguments, and index-in, index-out is how array recursions usually look.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.consequence: data = '1,2,#,#,3,#,#': integers pass by value in Python, so a child call's consumption never advances the caller's position — every level re-reads token 1 and the recursion spins or builds a wrong tree.
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.instead: Token consumption must be globally shared state: hand the recursion an iterator (next(tokens)) or a deque (popleft()), so each read permanently advances a single cursor. The stream-of-tokens framing is the fix, not a bigger integer.

Number of Islands.mistake: Flood-filling without marking cells at the moment they are discovered.
Number of Islands.why: Marking on arrival at a cell (when it is popped or recursed into) feels equivalent to marking when it is first seen.
Number of Islands.consequence: grid [['1', '1'], ['1', '1']]: neighbors re-add each other before either is marked — DFS recurses between cells endlessly, and BFS lets the queue balloon with duplicate entries on any large all-land grid.
Number of Islands.instead: Mark at discovery — flip the cell to '0' or record it visited when it is pushed, not when it is popped. The invariant everything in the queue is already marked is what bounds the work at one visit per cell.

Number of Islands.mistake: Incrementing the island count on every land cell encountered in the scan.
Number of Islands.why: Counting things is the task, and land cells are the things in view, so the counter gravitates to the wrong event.
Number of Islands.consequence: grid [['1', '1', '0'], ['0', '1', '0']]: three land cells produce a count of 3, but they are one connected island — the correct answer is 1.
Number of Islands.instead: Count discoveries of new components, not cells: increment only when the scan meets a land cell not yet absorbed, then flood-fill the entire component before scanning on. The flood-fill is what makes each island count exactly once.

Number of Islands.mistake: Including diagonal neighbors in the connectivity.
Number of Islands.why: Diagonal cells look adjacent on the grid picture, and eight-directional movement is common in other grid problems.
Number of Islands.consequence: grid [['1', '0'], ['0', '1']]: with diagonals the two cells fuse into one island and the answer comes out 1; the standard 4-directional definition gives 2.
Number of Islands.instead: Connectivity is defined by the problem, not by the picture — read the definition and confirm 4-directional aloud before coding the neighbor offsets. One clarifying sentence removes an entire class of wrong-answer submissions.

Rotten Oranges.mistake: Running BFS from one rotten orange at a time instead of all sources at once.
Rotten Oranges.why: BFS is taught single-source, so from each rotten orange, spread reads like the direct application of the tool.
Rotten Oranges.consequence: grid [[2, 1, 1, 1, 2]]: rot spreads from both ends simultaneously and finishes in 2 minutes, but a single-source pass from the left orange alone reports 3 — sequential sources overstate the time.
Rotten Oranges.instead: Simultaneity is modeled by seeding the queue with every initially rotten orange at time 0 — multi-source BFS. The wavefront then advances one minute per layer, which is exactly the physics the problem describes.

Rotten Oranges.mistake: Returning the elapsed minutes without checking whether fresh oranges survived.
Rotten Oranges.why: The BFS ran to completion, and a finished traversal feels like a finished problem.
Rotten Oranges.consequence: grid [[2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]: the fresh orange at the far corner is walled off and never rots — the correct answer is -1, but skipping the survivor check returns the minutes the reachable part took.
Rotten Oranges.instead: Count fresh oranges at the start, decrement on each rot, and let the final count decide: zero remaining means return the elapsed time, anything else means return -1. Unreachable targets are the standard trap in every spreading-process problem.

Rotten Oranges.mistake: Counting minutes per BFS layer in a way that includes the initial layer or the final empty one.
Rotten Oranges.why: Layer count and minute count feel identical, and on many grids they differ by exactly one in a way tests may not catch.
Rotten Oranges.consequence: grid [[2, 1, 1]]: the answer is 2, but incrementing the minute counter for the initial rotten layer (or after the last productive layer) reports 3.
Rotten Oranges.instead: Make time explicit instead of inferred: enqueue (cell, t) pairs, or increment only when a layer actually rots at least one fresh orange. Then verify on the smallest asymmetric grid, [[2, 1, 1]], where the answer must be 2.

Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.mistake: Using a single visited set and reporting a cycle on any revisit.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.why: That rule is correct for undirected graphs, and the undirected version is usually learned first, so it transfers silently.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.consequence: the diamond DAG edges = [[0, 1], [0, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]]: node 3 is reached along two different routes, the revisit fires, and an acyclic graph is reported cyclic.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.instead: Direction changes what a revisit means: only an edge back into the current recursion path proves a cycle. Keep two marks — visited (ever finished) and on-stack (in the active path) — and flag only on-stack revisits.

Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.mistake: Never removing nodes from the on-stack set when the recursion unwinds.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.why: Adding on entry is symmetric-feeling with adding to visited, and the removal has no analog in plain DFS to remind you.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.consequence: n = 3, edges = [[0, 1], [2, 1]]: after the walk 0 -> 1 finishes, node 1 stays flagged on-stack; the later walk from 2 reaches 1, sees the stale flag, and reports a cycle in an acyclic graph.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.instead: The on-stack set must mirror the call stack exactly — add on entry, remove on exit, no path spared. It is the same choose-explore-unchoose discipline as backtracking, applied to graph state.

Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.mistake: Launching DFS from node 0 only and trusting it to see the whole graph.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.why: Tree and grid problems usually have one natural root, and the habit of a single starting point carries over.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.consequence: n = 4, edges = [[2, 3], [3, 2]] with node 0 isolated: the search from 0 sees nothing, misses the 2 <-> 3 cycle entirely, and returns acyclic.
Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.instead: A directed graph has no reason to be reachable from any single vertex, so wrap the DFS in a loop over all unvisited nodes. The outer loop is part of the algorithm, not scaffolding.

Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).mistake: Returning the processed order without checking that it contains all n nodes.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).why: The queue drained and the loop ended cleanly, which feels like the algorithm declaring success.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).consequence: n = 2, edges = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]: both nodes start with nonzero in-degree (incoming edge count), the queue starts empty, and the loop exits at once — an empty order is returned as if valid, when the cycle means no order exists.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).instead: The length check is the cycle detector: a topological order exists exactly when processed == n. In Course Schedule terms, that comparison is the entire answer — say so explicitly rather than bolting on a separate cycle check.

Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).mistake: Building the adjacency and in-degrees with the prerequisite pairs read in the wrong direction.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).why: [a, b] gives no visual hint whether a needs b or b needs a, and both readings produce a running program.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).consequence: prerequisites = [[1, 0]] means course 0 comes before course 1 (edge 0 -> 1): with the direction flipped, the output order is [1, 0] — exactly backwards, on the simplest possible input.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).instead: Resolve the semantics on paper before coding: draw the two-node example, decide that [a, b] draws the edge b -> a (or the reverse, per the statement), and verify the tiny case end-to-end. Edge-direction bugs survive every test except the one you draw by hand.

Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).mistake: Enqueueing a neighbor every time its in-degree is decremented, rather than only when it reaches zero.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).why: Decrement and enqueue happen in the same breath of the algorithm's description, so the condition between them gets dropped.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).consequence: n = 3, edges = [[0, 2], [1, 2]]: node 2 is enqueued twice and appears twice in the output — the order has length 4 for a 3-node graph, breaking the count check and everything downstream.
Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).instead: In-degree zero is the event that means all prerequisites satisfied, and it happens exactly once per node — enqueue precisely at that moment. The guard is the algorithm's core claim, not an optimization.

Dijkstra's Algorithm.mistake: Running Dijkstra on a graph that contains negative edge weights.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.why: It is the shortest-path algorithm everyone reaches for, and nothing in the code visibly objects to a negative number.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.consequence: edges 0 -> 1 weight 1, 1 -> 2 weight -2, 0 -> 2 weight 0: node 2 is finalized at distance 0, but the path through node 1 costs -1 — the finalized answer is wrong and never revised.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.instead: Dijkstra's correctness rests on one claim: the smallest tentative distance can never improve later, which only holds when edges cannot subtract. Negative weights break the claim, so switch to Bellman-Ford — and say which assumption failed, because that is the real question.

Dijkstra's Algorithm.mistake: Processing every entry popped from the heap, with no staleness check.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.why: The heap only contains things the algorithm pushed, so everything in it feels legitimate to process.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.consequence: a node relaxed several times holds several heap entries, and only the smallest is current: on a graph with 10^5 edges, re-expanding stale entries multiplies the work and a comfortable O(E log V) run turns into a timeout.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.instead: Lazy deletion is the standard contract with a binary heap: on pop, compare the entry's distance with dist[u] and skip if it is worse. One if-statement stands in for the decrease-key operation the heap does not offer.

Dijkstra's Algorithm.mistake: Finalizing a node's distance at push time instead of pop time.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.why: The push happens at the moment of discovery, and discovery feels like the natural moment to lock in an answer.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.consequence: edges 0 -> 1 weight 10, 0 -> 2 weight 1, 2 -> 1 weight 1: node 1 is discovered first at distance 10; locking that in misses the cheaper route through node 2, and dist[1] stays 10 instead of 2.
Dijkstra's Algorithm.instead: A distance is proven minimal only when the node surfaces from the heap with the smallest tentative value — that surfacing is the proof. Push duplicates freely, finalize on pop, and let the staleness check absorb the redundancy.
